I was on deck when I felt her go over. It was not gradual. One moment we were upright, and inside twenty minutes we had seven degrees to starboard and the gangway was scraping the quay. I stopped the loading straight away and started transferring ballast from the starboard tanks to the port side. That took four hours. Nobody was hurt and we did not lose a single tonne of ore. What I still cannot explain is the plan. The manifest said the two holds nearest the bow first, and I watched the cranes start amidships. Somebody must have changed the sequence, and whoever changed it never told the bridge. The pilot had gone ashore before we opened the first hold, so there was nobody outside the ship to see it either.

When I board a ship I am not there to take her over. The master keeps command. What I bring is the water: I know where the bank is, where the current sets, and how the channel behaves on a falling tide. The first thing I ask for is the passage plan. I want to see every waypoint from the pilot station to the berth, with a time against it, and I want to know the draft the ship is leaving with, because that number decides everything else. If a waypoint on the plan does not match what I would do, we discuss it on the bridge before we move, not halfway down the channel. And if the plan has no waypoint for the turn into the basin, we make one. A plan that stops at the harbour entrance is not a plan.
